summary:
California's care-access law is the most protective element of its own record. Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 107 in September 2022, making California the first state to declare itself a sanctuary for transgender young people seeking medical care. Out-of-state youth can obtain hormones and puberty blockers in California, and the law shields families from child-abuse investigations or criminal prosecution for seeking gender-affirming care, including families who travel to California for it.

California's prison system is the one documented instance of identity-based placement in this inventory. As of January 2021 California is coded as the single state allowing transgender inmates to be housed according to their gender identity, with housing assigned identity-based within the general population and no trans-only separate facility documented. In 2015 California became the first state to fund gender-affirming surgeries for transgender prison inmates, and KPBS coverage of the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation's operational guidelines that year confirms the identity-based care and guidance posture while containing no explicit statement of a trans-only unit or segregation practice. The most recent documented statement of this housing practice in this record is dated January 2021; no later instance is documented.

Recorded hostility sits alongside that protective framework. The GLAAD ALERT Desk documented more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents nationwide in 2025, of which California recorded 198, the highest figure of any state. That ranking is by raw count only: the source supplies no population or per-capita denominator, so the count does not establish that California is riskier for an individual visitor than a smaller state.

A separate analysis of the same 2025 incident data reports a dramatic increase in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports in Los Angeles in law-enforcement data covering the same period as Governor Gavin Newsom's platforming of anti-trans figures.

A July 2026 analysis places California in the "Safest States" law band with a score of 4.1 and 1.9 recorded incidents, and argues that even the most protective statutory floors do not eliminate recorded hostility.
tangentialFactors:
The same 2025 national incident count that puts California at 198 records New Hampshire at 72, Texas at 66, Ohio at 50 and Washington at 50. The comparison is between raw counts across states of very different population sizes, and the source provides no per-capita adjustment.

California's prison housing posture is distinguished in the source from New Mexico, which is described as the one state maintaining separate facilities reserved for transgender people only. California's model is identity-based placement within the general population rather than a dedicated unit.

The July 2026 analysis sets California's 1.9 recorded incidents against its 4.1 protective-law score to argue that statutory protection and recorded hostility coexist, which bears on how much weight a visitor should place on the state's legal posture when judging day-to-day exposure.
localsOnly:
SB 107's shield operates for California families and for families who travel to the state for care, protecting them from child-abuse investigations and criminal prosecution over gender-affirming care sought for a young person.

Transgender people held in California prisons are housed according to their gender identity within the general population under corrections-department guidelines documented from 2015, and the state funds gender-affirming surgery for transgender inmates, a provision it introduced in 2015 as the first state to do so.

California recorded 198 of the more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents logged nationally in 2025, and Los Angeles saw a documented rise in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports to law enforcement over that period.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the identity-based prison housing policy documented as of January 2021 remains in force is unresolved in this inventory; no source dated after that point confirms or contradicts it, and no trans-only facility in California is documented either way.

The 198-incident figure for 2025 has no denominator in the sources, so its per-capita significance is unresolved; the ranking of states is by raw count only.

The methodology behind the July 2026 figures of a 4.1 law score and 1.9 recorded incidents is not stated in the inventory, including what the 1.9 counts or over what period.

No California-specific information is sourced here on facility or bathroom access, identity-document and gender-marker rules, entry screening, or hate-crime statute coverage; those layers sit in the national record or are not covered by this inventory.
